title: Why do balls dropped through pegs pile up in a bell shape?
checkedAgainst: Python's standard library, which `model.test.ts` runs through `oracle/galton.py` each time: `math.comb` for the number of routes to every bin of boards with 0 to 12 rows, `fractions.Fraction` for each bin's chance when a peg sends the ball right three times in four, and `statistics.NormalDist` for the bell curve's height and areas; `answers.ts` computes the check answers from the model. No physical board was measured.

grounding.subject: Python's math.comb and statistics.NormalDist, run by the model's tests
grounding.label: Run live: Python's math.comb and statistics.NormalDist, run by the model's tests
grounding.sentence: Checked live, each time the model’s tests run, against Python's math.comb and statistics.NormalDist, run by the model's tests.

answer: More routes lead to the middle bins than to the edges

questions.question: A smaller board has four rows of pegs, and one ball goes down every route. How many balls land in the middle bin, and why that many?
questions.answer: 6 of the 16. A route to the middle bin turns right at two of the four pegs, and there are 6 ways to choose which two; only 1 route, all lefts, reaches the left edge.

questions.question: On the six-row board a ball turns left, right, right, left, right, left. Which bin does it land in, and how many other routes end there?
questions.answer: The middle bin: it turned right 3 times, and a bin is the number of rights. 19 other routes end there, each with the same three rights in another order.

questions.question: Someone bends every peg so that a ball goes right three times in four. The routes are the same 64. Does the middle bin still collect the most balls?
questions.answer: No. The number of routes to each bin is unchanged, 20 to the middle, but the routes are no longer equally likely: every right is three times as likely as a left, so a route with more rights is more likely. The bin one from the right edge now collects the most, 35.6% of the balls, and the middle bin 13.2%.

steps.title: One ball, six coin flips
steps.line: At every peg the ball goes left or right.
steps.caption: A Galton board is a triangle of pegs over a row of bins. A ball dropped at the top hits a peg and falls to its left or its right, as likely one way as the other, then meets another peg. After six pegs it drops into one of seven bins. This ball went right 3 times and left 3 times, so it ends in the middle bin: a bin is the number of rights.
steps.picture: A triangle of pegs, 6 rows deep, over 7 bins; A ball that turns right, left, right, right, left, left and rests in the middle bin, its route drawn behind it; The route the ball took.

steps.title: One ball down every route: which bin fills highest?
steps.line: Predict: an edge bin, the middle bin, or all the same?
steps.caption: Six pegs, two ways at each: 64 different routes from the top to the bins, each as likely as any other. The arcs show every hop a ball could make. Drop exactly one ball down each of the 64 routes. Will the balls spread evenly over the seven bins, pile up at an edge, or pile up in the middle?
steps.picture: A triangle of pegs, 6 rows deep, over 7 bins; An arc for every hop a ball could make: two from each peg; 4 labels. New in this step: An arc for every hop a ball could make: two from each peg; 4 labels.

steps.title: The middle bin gets 20 balls, each edge bin 1
steps.line: More routes lead to the middle bins than to the edges.
steps.caption: No ball was steered. Each of the 64 routes carried one ball, and 20 of those routes end in the middle bin while only 1 ends in each edge bin. More routes lead to the middle bins than to the edges, and since every route is equally likely, a ball is 20 times as likely to finish in the middle as at the far left.
steps.picture: A triangle of pegs, 6 rows deep, over 7 bins; An arc for every hop a ball could make: two from each peg; 64 balls dropped, one down every route; 7 labels. New in this step: 64 balls dropped, one down every route; 7 labels.

steps.title: One way to reach the edge, 20 ways to reach the middle
steps.line: A bin is a number of rights; a route is one order for them.
steps.caption: To reach the left edge a ball must go left at all six pegs: one route. To reach the middle it needs three rights and three lefts, in any order, and there are 20 different orders: rights first, lefts first, or mixed. Drawn over the pegs are the one route down the left side and three of the 20 that end in the middle. The pile is a count of orders.
steps.picture: A triangle of pegs, 6 rows deep, over 7 bins; The one route to the left edge bin, down the left side, and three of the 20 routes to the middle bin; 14 labels. New in this step: The one route to the left edge bin, down the left side, and three of the 20 routes to the middle bin; Left edge bin: 1 route; LLLLLL; and 5 more.

steps.title: A bell curve fits the pile
steps.line: Bins inside the brace: 78.1% counted, 77.9% under the curve.
steps.caption: The smooth line is the normal curve, the bell curve, drawn with the pile’s own middle and spread. It was not used to make the pile; it is laid over it. The three bins inside the brace hold 50 of the 64 balls, 78.1%. The shaded area under the curve across the same three bins is 77.9% of the curve’s whole area: the same share to within a quarter of a percentage point.
steps.picture: A triangle of pegs, 6 rows deep, over 7 bins; A bell curve over the pile, shaded across the three middle bins; A brace under the three middle bins: 50 of 64 balls, 78.1% counted and 77.9% under the curve; 7 labels. New in this step: A bell curve over the pile, shaded across the three middle bins; A brace under the three middle bins: 50 of 64 balls, 78.1% counted and 77.9% under the curve.

steps.title: At the edges the curve drifts from the count
steps.line: The board ends at its last bin; the curve runs on past it.
steps.caption: The curve is an approximation, and the edges show it. One route in 64 reaches the left edge bin, 1.56% of the balls; the curve gives that bin 1.85%. The curve also keeps going past the last bin, putting 0.21% of its area on each side where the board has no bins at all. Use the curve for the middle of a pile like this, and count routes at its edges.
steps.picture: Left edge bin: 1 route in 64. 1.56%. Left edge bin, under the curve. 1.85%. Past the last bin, under the curve. 0.21%.
